title: Atoms, molecules and stoichiometry
objectives: Define the unified atomic mass unit, relative atomic mass, relative isotopic mass, relative molecular mass and relative formula mass
Define the mole using the Avogadro constant, and convert between mass, amount, number of particles, gas volume and solution concentration
Write formulas of ionic compounds from ionic charges and oxidation numbers, and recall the formulas of common ions
Write and balance full and ionic equations with state symbols
Define and calculate empirical and molecular formulas; use the terms anhydrous, hydrated and water of crystallisation
Carry out reacting-mass, gas-volume, solution, limiting-reagent and percentage-yield calculations to the correct significant figures
prior: Relative formula mass from the Periodic Table
Ions and their charges for Groups 1, 2, 16 and 17
why: Stoichiometry is the arithmetic of chemistry. Almost every calculation in AS Chemistry, from enthalpy changes and titrations to equilibrium constants, starts by converting something into moles. Paper 1 usually has three or four questions on this chapter, and Paper 2 nearly always includes a multi-step mole calculation.
intro: Atoms are far too small to count one by one, so chemists count them in moles. In this chapter you will learn how to compare the masses of atoms, how the mole links mass to numbers of particles, how to write formulas and equations correctly, and how to use them to predict the amounts of substances that react and form.

sections.title: Relative masses of atoms and molecules

blocks.h: Atoms are so light that grams are a useless unit for them. Instead, masses are compared with the carbon-12 atom, which is the agreed standard.
One twelfth of the mass of one atom of carbon-12.
The mass of one atom of an isotope compared with one twelfth of the mass of an atom of carbon-12 (i.e. measured in unified atomic mass units).
The weighted average mass of the atoms of an element (taking account of the abundances of its isotopes) compared with one twelfth of the mass of an atom of carbon-12.
The weighted average mass of a molecule compared with one twelfth of the mass of an atom of carbon-12. Used for covalent (molecular) substances.

The weighted average mass of one formula unit compared with one twelfth of the mass of an atom of carbon-12. Used for ionic compounds and giant structures, e.g. NaCl, SiO<sub>2</sub>. (It is also written M<sub>r</sub>.)
Relative masses have no units, because they are ratios. A relative isotopic mass is close to a whole number (35Cl ≈ 35.0); a relative atomic mass is an average and usually is not (Cl = 35.5).

blocks.err: Adding the isotopic masses and halving: 36.0 ignores the abundances.

blocks.wrong: The relative molecular mass of NaCl is 58.5.
blocks.right: NaCl is ionic and has no molecules: use relative formula mass. Examiners check this word.

o: The relative isotopic mass of <sup>24</sup>Mg is 24.3
The relative formula mass of CaCO<sub>3</sub> is 100.1
One unified atomic mass unit is the mass of a hydrogen atom
blocks.why: Ca 40.1 + C 12.0 + 3 × 16.0 = 100.1. A<sub>r</sub>(O) is 16.0; 24.3 is A<sub>r</sub>(Mg), an average; 1 u is 1/12 of a <sup>12</sup>C atom.

sections.title: The mole and the Avogadro constant

blocks.h: The amount of substance that contains 6.02 × 10<sup>23</sup> particles (the Avogadro constant, L or N<sub>A</sub>). One mole of a substance has a mass in grams equal to its relative atomic, molecular or formula mass.
amount (mol) = mass (g) ÷ M (g mol<sup>−1</sup>)     number of particles = amount × L
Always say which particles you are counting. One mole of CO2 contains 1 mol of molecules, 1 mol of C atoms, 2 mol of O atoms and 3 mol of atoms in total.

blocks.q: How many oxygen atoms are in 8.80 g of carbon dioxide? (L = 6.02 × 10<sup>23</sup> mol<sup>−1</sup>)
blocks.err: Forgetting the factor of 2 for the two O atoms in each molecule.

blocks.h: Gas volumes
Equal volumes of all gases at the same temperature and pressure contain the same number of molecules. At room conditions (as given in the Data Booklet) one mole of any gas occupies 24.0 dm3.
amount of gas (mol) = volume (dm<sup>3</sup>) ÷ 24.0   (room conditions)     1 dm<sup>3</sup> = 1000 cm<sup>3</sup>
For gases at other conditions you use the ideal gas equation, pV = nRT, which is covered in Chapter 4.
Solutions
amount (mol) = concentration (mol dm<sup>−3</sup>) × volume (dm<sup>3</sup>)     volume in dm<sup>3</sup> = cm<sup>3</sup> ÷ 1000

Concentration may also be given in g dm<sup>−3</sup>: mass concentration = molar concentration × M. When a solution is diluted, the amount of solute stays the same: c<sub>1</sub>V<sub>1</sub> = c<sub>2</sub>V<sub>2</sub>.

blocks.name: moles
blocks.title: Mole calculator
blocks.h: Type any formula, such as CuSO4.5H2O or Ca(OH)2. Then convert between mass, amount, particles, gas volume and solution concentration, with every step of the working shown.
Write the unit after every number in your working, and convert cm<sup>3</sup> to dm<sup>3</sup> before using concentration. Most lost marks in mole calculations are unit slips, not chemistry.
Formulas of ionic compounds

In an ionic compound the total positive charge equals the total negative charge. Predict simple ion charges from the Periodic Table: Group 1 → 1+, Group 2 → 2+, Group 13 → 3+ (Al<sup>3+</sup>), Group 15 → 3− (N<sup>3−</sup>), Group 16 → 2−, Group 17 → 1−. A Roman numeral gives the oxidation number of a metal with more than one ion: iron(III) is Fe<sup>3+</sup>, copper(II) is Cu<sup>2+</sup>.

blocks.q: Write the formula of ammonium phosphate and of iron(III) sulfate.
steps: NH4+ and PO43−: three NH4+ balance one PO43− → (NH4)3PO4
Fe3+ and SO42−: lowest common multiple of 3 and 2 is 6 → 2 Fe3+ and 3 SO42− → Fe2(SO4)3
blocks.err: Writing NH<sub>4</sub>3PO<sub>4</sub> without brackets, or FeSO<sub>4</sub> (that is iron(II) sulfate).

blocks.q: Match each compound to its formula:

blocks.h: Equations and ionic equations

A balanced equation has the same number of atoms of each element on both sides; for ionic equations the total charge must also balance. Use state symbols: (s), (l), (g), (aq). In an ionic equation, leave out spectator ions: ions that are unchanged by the reaction.

blocks.q: Write the ionic equation for the reaction of aqueous silver nitrate with aqueous sodium chloride.
steps: Full equation: AgNO<sub>3</sub>(aq) + NaCl(aq) → AgCl(s) + NaNO<sub>3</sub>(aq)
Ions present: Ag<sup>+</sup>, NO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>, Na<sup>+</sup>, Cl<sup>−</sup>. Na<sup>+</sup> and NO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> stay in solution unchanged: spectators
blocks.err: Including Na<sup>+</sup> and NO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>, or giving AgCl the state (aq).

blocks.q: Balance the complete combustion of butane, C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>.
blocks.err: Balancing O before C and H. Always do the element in only one product first.

blocks.h: Empirical and molecular formulas
The simplest whole-number ratio of the atoms of each element present in a compound.
The actual number of atoms of each element in one molecule of a compound. It is a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula.

blocks.q: A compound contains 40.0% C, 6.7% H and 53.3% O by mass, and M<sub>r</sub> = 180. Find its empirical and molecular formulas.
steps: Divide by the smallest (3.33): C 1, H 2.0, O 1 → empirical formula CH2O (M = 30.0)
blocks.err: Rounding 1.5 to 2 instead of doubling every value (a ratio of 1 : 1.5 means 2 : 3).

blocks.h: If you are given combustion data instead of percentages: all the C ends up in CO<sub>2</sub> (mass C = mass CO<sub>2</sub> × 12.0/44.0) and all the H in H<sub>2</sub>O (mass H = mass H<sub>2</sub>O × 2.0/18.0). Find O by difference.
Water of crystallisation
Water molecules that are chemically bound into the crystal structure of a salt, e.g. CuSO4•5H2O. A salt that contains it is hydrated; one without it is anhydrous.

blocks.q: Heating 2.50 g of hydrated copper(II) sulfate, CuSO<sub>4</sub>•xH<sub>2</sub>O, to constant mass leaves 1.60 g of anhydrous CuSO<sub>4</sub>. Find x.
blocks.err: Using the mass of the hydrated salt with the M<sub>r</sub> of the anhydrous salt.

blocks.h: Heat to constant mass (repeat heating and weighing until the mass stops changing) so that you know all the water has gone.
Every stoichiometry problem follows the same route: convert what you know into moles → use the equation's mole ratio → convert moles into what you want.

blocks.q: What mass of calcium oxide is produced when 25.0 g of calcium carbonate is heated? CaCO<sub>3</sub> → CaO + CO<sub>2</sub>
steps: Ratio CaCO<sub>3</sub> : CaO = 1 : 1, so n(CaO) = 0.250 mol

blocks.h: Percentage yield
percentage yield = (actual mass of product ÷ theoretical maximum mass) × 100
Yields are below 100% because of incomplete or reversible reactions, side reactions and losses when transferring and purifying the product.
Limiting and excess reagents

The limiting reagent is the reactant that is used up first; it decides the amount of product. To find it, compare the moles of each reactant divided by its number in the equation: the smaller value is limiting.

blocks.q: 2.43 g of magnesium is added to 100 cm<sup>3</sup> of 1.00 mol dm<sup>−3</sup> hydrochloric acid. Mg + 2HCl → MgCl<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>. What volume of hydrogen forms at room conditions?
steps: Divide by coefficients: Mg 0.100 ÷ 1 = 0.100; HCl 0.100 ÷ 2 = 0.0500 → HCl is limiting
blocks.err: Using the magnesium (0.100 mol) and getting 2.40 dm<sup>3</sup>.

blocks.h: Gas volumes in reactions

For reacting gases at the same temperature and pressure, volumes are in the same ratio as moles, so you can use the equation's coefficients directly on volumes. Water is a liquid at room temperature, so it does not count in a final gas volume. Aqueous alkali (NaOH or KOH) absorbs CO2 (and SO2).

blocks.q: 20 cm<sup>3</sup> of methane is burned in 100 cm<sup>3</sup> of oxygen. What is the final gas volume at room temperature and pressure, and what volume remains after passing through NaOH(aq)?
steps: 20 cm<sup>3</sup> CH<sub>4</sub> uses 40 cm<sup>3</sup> O<sub>2</sub> → 60 cm<sup>3</sup> O<sub>2</sub> left over; 20 cm<sup>3</sup> CO<sub>2</sub> forms
Final gas = 60 + 20 = 80 cm3; after NaOH, the CO2 is absorbed → 60 cm3 (oxygen)

blocks.h: Titrations

blocks.q: 25.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of sodium hydroxide is neutralised by 20.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of 0.150 mol dm<sup>−3</sup> sulfuric acid. Find the concentration of the NaOH.

blocks.h: Give your final answer to the same number of significant figures as the least precise data in the question (usually 3). Do not round intermediate values; keep them in your calculator.

blocks.name: stoich
blocks.title: Calculation trainer
blocks.h: Unlimited practice with new numbers every time: reacting masses, gas volumes, titrations, limiting reagents, percentage yield and empirical formulas. Enter your answer, then see the full working.

blocks.wrong: The reactant with fewer moles is always the limiting reagent.
blocks.right: Compare moles divided by the coefficients in the equation. 0.10 mol HCl is limiting against 0.10 mol Mg because HCl reacts 2 : 1.

summary: 1 u = 1/12 of the mass of a <sup>12</sup>C atom. A<sub>r</sub> is a weighted average of isotopic masses; use "relative formula mass" for ionic compounds.
Gases at room conditions: n = V(dm<sup>3</sup>) ÷ 24.0. Solutions: n = c × V(dm<sup>3</sup>); dilution keeps n constant.

Ionic formulas balance charge; know NO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>, CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2−</sup>, SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup>, OH<sup>−</sup>, NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>, Zn<sup>2+</sup>, Ag<sup>+</sup>, HCO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>, PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3−</sup>.
Balance atoms (and charge); ionic equations omit spectator ions; always include state symbols when asked.
Empirical formula: mass ÷ A<sub>r</sub> → divide by smallest → whole numbers. Molecular formula = n × empirical formula.
Hydrated salts contain water of crystallisation; heat to constant mass to find x.
Route for every calculation: known → moles → mole ratio → required quantity.
Limiting reagent: smallest (moles ÷ coefficient). Percentage yield = actual ÷ theoretical × 100.
Gas volumes react in the same ratio as moles (same T and p); water is liquid at room temperature.
Answers to the number of significant figures justified by the data.

flash.q: Define the unified atomic mass unit.
flash.a: 1/12 of the mass of one atom of carbon-12
Weighted average mass of the atoms of an element compared with 1/12 of the mass of a carbon-12 atom

flash.q: Relative isotopic mass vs relative atomic mass?
flash.a: Isotopic: one isotope (≈ whole number). Atomic: weighted average of all isotopes

flash.q: When do you say "relative formula mass"?
flash.a: For ionic compounds and giant structures (no molecules)
Amount containing 6.02 × 10²³ particles (the Avogadro constant)

flash.q: Molar gas volume at room conditions?
flash.a: 24.0 dm³ mol⁻¹
n = c × V, with V in dm³
PO₄³⁻
HCO₃⁻

An ion present in the reaction mixture that is unchanged by the reaction

Actual number of atoms of each element in one molecule
CH₂O
Water molecules bound into the crystal structure of a hydrated salt
To make sure all the water of crystallisation has been removed

flash.a: Compare moles ÷ coefficient for each reactant; the smallest is limiting
actual ÷ theoretical × 100
Incomplete/reversible reactions, side reactions, losses in transfer and purification

flash.a: mass CO₂ × 12.0/44.0
mass H₂O × 2.0/18.0
At the same T and p, volumes react in the same ratio as the coefficients

flash.a: Aqueous NaOH or KOH

practice.q: Boron has two isotopes, <sup>10</sup>B (19.9%) and <sup>11</sup>B (80.1%). Calculate A<sub>r</sub>(B) to 3 s.f.
Calculate the number of ions in 5.85 g of sodium chloride.
practice.a: n(NaCl) = 5.85 ÷ 58.5 = 0.100 mol; each formula unit has 2 ions → 0.200 × 6.02 × 10<sup>23</sup> = 1.20 × 10<sup>23</sup> ions

practice.q: Write the ionic equation, with state symbols, for the neutralisation of any strong acid by any strong alkali.
10.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of 2.00 mol dm<sup>−3</sup> HCl is diluted to 250 cm<sup>3</sup>. Find the new concentration.
6.40 g of copper is heated in air to give 7.20 g of an oxide. Find its empirical formula.
4.0 g of hydrogen reacts with 16.0 g of oxygen to make water. Which reagent is in excess, and by how many grams?
practice.a: n(H<sub>2</sub>) = 2.0 mol needs 1.0 mol O<sub>2</sub> (32.0 g); only 0.50 mol O<sub>2</sub> is present, so O<sub>2</sub> is limiting. H<sub>2</sub> used = 1.0 mol = 2.0 g → 2.0 g of H<sub>2</sub> in excess.

assessment.q: What is the relative formula mass of hydrated sodium carbonate, Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>•10H<sub>2</sub>O?
How many moles of atoms are there in 0.50 mol of ammonium sulfate?
What volume of oxygen at room conditions is needed to burn 0.10 mol of propane completely?
Which is the formula of iron(III) hydrogencarbonate?

20.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of 0.100 mol dm<sup>−3</sup> Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> is titrated with 0.200 mol dm<sup>−3</sup> HCl. What volume of HCl is needed? Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> + 2HCl → 2NaCl + CO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O
A hydrocarbon has empirical formula CH<sub>2</sub> and M<sub>r</sub> = 70. What is its molecular formula?
The theoretical yield of a product is 8.00 g but 6.40 g is obtained. What is the percentage yield?
Which is the ionic equation for the precipitation of barium sulfate from BaCl<sub>2</sub>(aq) and Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>(aq)?
assessment.why: Na<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>−</sup> are spectators; BaSO<sub>4</sub> is a solid precipitate.

assessment.q: 1.00 g of each gas is collected at room conditions. Which has the largest volume?
assessment.why: Smallest M<sub>r</sub> (16.0) gives the most moles and so the largest volume.

assessment.q: 0.500 mol of Al reacts with 0.600 mol of Cl<sub>2</sub>: 2Al + 3Cl<sub>2</sub> → 2AlCl<sub>3</sub>. What amount of AlCl<sub>3</sub> forms?

assessment_s.q:
Limestone is mainly calcium carbonate. A 2.50 g sample of limestone reacts with an excess of hydrochloric acid, producing 528 cm3 of CO2 at room conditions.
(a) Write the equation, with state symbols. [2]
(b) Calculate the amount of CO2 produced. [1]
(c) Calculate the percentage by mass of CaCO3 in the limestone. [2]
assessment_s.a:
(a) CaCO3(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl2(aq) + H2O(l) + CO2(g) [1 equation, 1 state symbols]
(b) 0.528 ÷ 24.0 = 0.0220 mol
(c) mass CaCO3 = 0.0220 × 100.1 = 2.20 g; 2.20 ÷ 2.50 × 100 = 88.1%

assessment_s.q:
A compound of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen only: 0.600 g burns completely to give 0.880 g of CO2 and 0.360 g of H2O. Mr = 60.0.
(a) Calculate the masses of C, H and O in the sample. [2]
(b) Deduce the empirical and molecular formulas. [2]

pp.mis: Using one K instead of two in K₂CO₃
pp.stem: Which potassium compound contains 52.4% by mass of potassium?

pp.mis: Using M(SO₂) for sulfur, or S = 16
pp.stem: A sample of coal contains 1.284 g of sulfur. What is the maximum volume of sulfur dioxide, measured at room conditions, produced when the coal burns completely?

pp.mis: Forgetting the O already in the alcohol
pp.stem: How many moles of oxygen gas are needed for the complete combustion of 1 mol of propan-1-ol, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH?
pp.exp: C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O + 4.5O<sub>2</sub> → 3CO<sub>2</sub> + 4H<sub>2</sub>O. Products contain 6 + 4 = 10 O atoms; the alcohol supplies 1, so 9 O atoms = 4.5 O<sub>2</sub>.

wrong.D: ignored the O in the alcohol
wrong.C: counted O atoms, not O₂ molecules

pp.stem:
An excess of copper(II) carbonate, CuCO3 (Mr = 123.5), is added to acid.
CuCO3 + 2HCl → CuCl2 + H2O + CO2
5.00 g of CuCO3 is added to 25.0 cm3 of 2.00 mol dm−3 HCl. What mass of CuCO3 is left unreacted?
pp.exp: n(HCl) = 2.00 × 0.0250 = 0.0500 mol, which reacts with 0.0250 mol CuCO<sub>3</sub> = 3.09 g. Left: 5.00 − 3.09 = 1.91 g.

pp.mis: Not writing the balanced equation first
pp.stem: Potassium carbonate neutralises phosphoric acid, producing potassium phosphate, carbon dioxide and water only. What volume of 0.40 mol dm<sup>−3</sup> K<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> exactly neutralises 20.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of 0.30 mol dm<sup>−3</sup> H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub>?
pp.exp: 3K<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> + 2H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub> → 2K<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub> + 3CO<sub>2</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub>O. n(H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub>) = 6.00 × 10<sup>−3</sup> mol → n(K<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>) = 9.00 × 10<sup>−3</sup> mol → V = 0.0225 dm<sup>3</sup> = 22.5 cm<sup>3</sup>.

pp.stem: Which equation describes the complete combustion of an alkane, C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub>?
pp.exp: n C atoms → nCO<sub>2</sub>; (2n+2) H atoms → (n+1)H<sub>2</sub>O. O atoms needed = 2n + n + 1 = 3n + 1, i.e. ½(3n+1) O<sub>2</sub>. Check with methane (n = 1): CH<sub>4</sub> + 2O<sub>2</sub> → CO<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O.

pp.mis: Forgetting to convert cm³ to dm³
pp.stem: Sample X is added to water and the solution is made up to 250 cm<sup>3</sup>. This gives 0.200 mol dm<sup>−3</sup> NaOH. What is X?
pp.exp: Needed: 0.200 × 0.250 = 0.0500 mol. Only 100 cm<sup>3</sup> × 0.50 mol dm<sup>−3</sup> = 0.0500 mol matches (A 0.025, B 0.10, D 0.025).

pp.stem: A mixture of 20 cm<sup>3</sup> of propane and 10 cm<sup>3</sup> of ethene is sparked with an excess of oxygen. After cooling to room temperature, the remaining gas is passed through aqueous sodium hydroxide. All volumes are measured at the same temperature and pressure. What volume of gas is absorbed by the alkali?
pp.exp: NaOH absorbs CO<sub>2</sub>. C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub> gives 3 × 20 = 60 cm<sup>3</sup> CO<sub>2</sub>; C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub> gives 2 × 10 = 20 cm<sup>3</sup>. Total 80 cm<sup>3</sup>.

pp.stem: Which pair of formulae is correct?
pp.exp: Zn<sup>2+</sup> needs two OH<sup>−</sup>; two NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> balance SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup>. In C, (NH<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub> is right but zinc nitrate is Zn(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>; in D, AgNO<sub>3</sub> and NaHCO<sub>3</sub>.

pp.mis: Counting molecules when atoms are asked for
pp.stem: How many atoms are present in 64.2 g of solid sulfur, S<sub>8</sub>? (L = the Avogadro constant)
pp.exp: 64.2 g ÷ 32.1 g mol<sup>−1</sup> = 2.00 mol of S atoms = 2L atoms. (It is 0.250 mol of S<sub>8</sub> molecules, i.e. L/4 molecules: option A is the trap.)

pp.stem: Y is an impure sample of a Group 2 carbonate, MCO<sub>3</sub>. Y contains 60% MCO<sub>3</sub> by mass; the impurities do not react with acid. 12.3 g of Y reacts with an excess of dilute hydrochloric acid, producing 0.0500 mol of carbon dioxide. What is M?
pp.exp: Mass of MCO<sub>3</sub> = 0.60 × 12.3 = 7.38 g = 0.0500 mol, so M(MCO<sub>3</sub>) = 147.6. A<sub>r</sub>(M) = 147.6 − 60.0 = 87.6: strontium.

pp.stem: Which sample contains the same number of atoms as 4.0 g of helium? (M<sub>r</sub>: O<sub>2</sub> 32.0, H<sub>2</sub>O 18.0, CO<sub>2</sub> 44.0, NH<sub>3</sub> 17.0)
pp.exp: 4.0 g He = 1.0 mol of atoms. 16 g O<sub>2</sub> = 0.50 mol molecules × 2 = 1.0 mol atoms. B and C have 3 mol of atoms, D has 4 mol.

pp.stem: Compound R contains only C, H and O. 3.00 g of R contains 1.20 g of carbon and 0.20 g of hydrogen. R reacts with aqueous sodium carbonate to give bubbles of gas. What is R?
pp.exp: O = 3.00 − 1.40 = 1.60 g. Moles C 0.100 : H 0.20 : O 0.100 → empirical formula CH<sub>2</sub>O. Fizzing with Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> shows a carboxylic acid: ethanoic acid, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>O<sub>2</sub>. HCHO and HCOOCH<sub>3</sub> also fit CH<sub>2</sub>O but are not acids.

pp.stem:
BaS2O6•2H2O (Mr = 333.5) dissolves in acid and slowly decomposes: S2O62−(aq) → SO2(g) + SO42−(aq). The sulfate formed precipitates as BaSO4 (Mr = 233.4).
3.335 g of BaS2O6•2H2O is made up to 250 cm3. Later, 0.467 g of BaSO4 has formed. What is the concentration of BaS2O6 remaining?
pp.exp: Start: 3.335 ÷ 333.5 = 0.0100 mol. BaSO<sub>4</sub>: 0.467 ÷ 233.4 = 0.00200 mol, so 0.00200 mol has decomposed. Remaining 0.00800 mol ÷ 0.250 dm<sup>3</sup> = 0.0320 mol dm<sup>−3</sup>.

pp.mis: Mixing up hydrated and anhydrous masses
pp.stem: Hydrated magnesium sulfate, MgSO<sub>4</sub>•xH<sub>2</sub>O, is heated to constant mass. Mass of empty crucible = Q g; crucible + hydrated salt = R g; crucible + residue = S g. M<sub>r</sub>(MgSO<sub>4</sub>) = 120.4. Which expression gives x?
pp.exp: Water lost = R − S, so n(H<sub>2</sub>O) = (R − S)/18. Anhydrous MgSO<sub>4</sub> = S − Q, so n(MgSO<sub>4</sub>) = (S − Q)/120.4. x = ratio = 120.4(R − S) ÷ 18(S − Q).

pp.stem: What is the empirical formula of hexanedioic acid, HOOC(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>4</sub>COOH?
pp.exp: Molecular formula C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>4</sub>; divide by 2 → C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O<sub>2</sub>.

pp.stem: Tartaric acid, HOOCCH(OH)CH(OH)COOH, is the only acid in a sample of grape juice. The juice reacts completely with 50.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of 0.40 mol dm<sup>−3</sup> sodium carbonate, with no carbonate left over. What amount of tartaric acid was in the juice?
pp.exp: Tartaric acid has two COOH groups (H<sub>2</sub>A): H<sub>2</sub>A + Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> → Na<sub>2</sub>A + CO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O. n(Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>) = 0.020 mol = n(acid). The OH groups are alcohol groups and do not react with carbonate.

pp.stem: Which statement is correct?
opts: One unified atomic mass unit is one twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
The relative atomic mass of chlorine is 71.0.
The relative molecular mass of potassium bromide is 119.0.
The relative isotopic mass of <sup>12</sup>C is 12.011.
pp.exp: A is the definition. Cl has A<sub>r</sub> 35.5 (71.0 is Cl<sub>2</sub>); KBr is ionic, so "relative formula mass"; <sup>12</sup>C has relative isotopic mass exactly 12.

pp.stem: Which compound has the empirical formula C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>O?
pp.exp: Butanoic acid C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>2</sub> → C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>O. Ethanoic acid → CH<sub>2</sub>O; propan-1-ol C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O; methyl ethanoate C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O<sub>2</sub>.

pp.stem: What mass of iron is needed to produce 0.050 mol of iron(III) oxide, Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>?
pp.exp: Each Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> contains 2 Fe: n(Fe) = 0.100 mol × 55.8 = 5.58 g.

pp.stem: Compound Z contains C, H and O only. 1.50 g of Z burns completely to give 2.20 g of CO<sub>2</sub> and 0.90 g of H<sub>2</sub>O. What is the empirical formula of Z?

pp.mis: Losing track of the ratio between stages
pp.stem:
Iron is extracted from pyrite, FeS2, in two stages.
• 4FeS2 + 11O2 → 2Fe2O3 + 8SO2
• Fe2O3 + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO2
What is the maximum volume of CO2, at room conditions, produced in stage 2 from 10 mol of FeS2?
pp.exp: 10 mol FeS<sub>2</sub> → 5 mol Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> → 15 mol CO<sub>2</sub> × 24.0 = 360 dm<sup>3</sup>.

pp.stem: Hydrogen sulfide burns in oxygen to form sulfur dioxide and steam. How many moles of oxygen are needed to convert 8.0 mol of hydrogen sulfide?
pp.exp: 2H<sub>2</sub>S + 3O<sub>2</sub> → 2SO<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O, so O<sub>2</sub> = 1.5 × 8.0 = 12.0 mol.

pp.mis: Balancing one element at a time without rechecking
pp.stem: In the equation 4NH<sub>3</sub> + x NO → y N<sub>2</sub> + z H<sub>2</sub>O, what are x, y and z?
pp.exp: H: 12 H → z = 6. O: x = z = 6. N: 4 + 6 = 10 → y = 5. Check: 4NH<sub>3</sub> + 6NO → 5N<sub>2</sub> + 6H<sub>2</sub>O.

pp.stem: A 0.640 g sample of calcium carbide reacts with excess water; ethyne is the only carbon-containing product. The ethyne burns completely to give 480 cm<sup>3</sup> of CO<sub>2</sub> at room conditions. What is the formula of calcium carbide?
In a reaction between two gases, three reactant molecules produce two product molecules. What could the two gases be?
pp.exp: 2CO + O<sub>2</sub> → 2CO<sub>2</sub> (3 → 2). N<sub>2</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub> → 2NH<sub>3</sub> (4 → 2); H<sub>2</sub> + Cl<sub>2</sub> → 2HCl (2 → 2); N<sub>2</sub> + O<sub>2</sub> → 2NO (2 → 2).

pp.stem: What contains 1.204 × 10<sup>24</sup> oxygen atoms?

Carbon monoxide reacts with steam: CO(g) + H<sub>2</sub>O(g) → CO<sub>2</sub>(g) + H<sub>2</sub>(g). 2.80 g of CO and 2.70 g of steam react until one is used up. What volume of hydrogen forms at room conditions?
pp.exp: CO 0.100 mol; H<sub>2</sub>O 0.150 mol → CO limiting → 0.100 mol H<sub>2</sub> × 24.0 = 2.40 dm<sup>3</sup>.
